extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent examiners, patent agents, and applicants (prosecution before CIPO)
extracted.subtask_description: Official Canadian Patent Office guidance on examination, reporting, searching, abstracts, disclosure, requisitions, interviews, and related procedural and substantive requirements for patent applications filed or entering national phase in Canada.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) is the reference skilled addressee used to assess disclosure, obviousness, and other issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual uses examples to identify the POSITA for particular scenarios (e.g., 'The POSITA is the same as that of Example 3, Scenario a) above'). Examiners may set out the POSITA in reports where there is disagreement about claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common General Knowledge (CGK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common general knowledge consists of what is generally known and accepted by the POSITA in the relevant field at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: board games, a particular 3-dimensional board, pieces, mechanized arm and claw, and hydraulic pistons per se can be CGK depending on the field. The examiner may identify CGK in the report to support claim construction and patentability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution analysis and identification of essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should identify the problem outlined in the description, the solution contemplated by the inventor, and the essential elements that lead to that solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language used in reports: state the problem (e.g., 'finding an improved method of playing the game'), set out the solution (e.g., 'inclusion of hydraulic pistons at each corner'), and distinguish contextual features from essential elements (e.g., the board, pieces, arm and claw provide context but the hydraulic pistons are the essential elements). This analysis supports determinations such as statutory subject-matter and claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory character of the claim (is the claim statutory?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the essential elements provide a new practical application and thereby constitute statutory subject-matter under the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In examples the manual concludes 'Yes' where the essential elements (e.g., hydraulic pistons allowing board tilting) provide a new practical application to a context (e.g., a game board). Examiners should explain the essential elements and why they render the claim statutory or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes all information made available to the public anywhere before the claim date (subject to limited exceptions). Search scope should identify relevant prior art for patentability assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, prior art relied on includes published patent documents, journal articles, textbooks, manuals, etc. The scope of a Canadian examiner's search depends partly on earlier searches; examiners are not required to search claimed matter having defects (unity, divisional, new matter). Even where an International Searching Authority performed a comprehensive search, a Canadian examiner will at minimum search Canadian patent documents (e.g., for double-patenting or anticipation). Examiners should consider available foreign search results and, if relying on them in a report, indicate which documents were identified. Further searches may be undertaken when appropriate and need not be limited to Canadian documents; searches are generally limited by dates, keywords, and IPC codes. Examiners should aim to identify all relevant prior art in the first report but acknowledge documents may be missed; if relevant prior art is identified later, the examiner must cite it against the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and form of an examiner's report
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's report is a notice identifying defects in the application and containing a requisition under subsection 86(2) or 86(5) of the Patent Rules; it communicates defects and related requisitions to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A requisition typically begins with language like 'The examiner has identified the following defects in the application' and ends with language requiring amendment or argument. Reports may include additional informative content: date and origin of recent amendments, number of claims on file, statement regarding the search performed, identification and discussion of prior art, general prosecution comments, and the examiner's view of POSITA, CGK, problem, solution, and essential elements. Reports should be as comprehensive as possible to enable informed prosecution decisions. A Final Action is a specific report issued when prosecution appears to have reached an impasse. Examiners do not issue reports when the application is compliant or contains only minor defects; in such cases the examiner will approve the application for allowance or issue a conditional notice of allowance. Separate requisitions under sections 85 and 94 may be included; requirements to request continued examination under section 85.1 may be included as informative statements. Each separate requisition and any separate requirement must be responded to within the time period indicated or the application will be abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisitions concerning foreign applications (section 85)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the examiner has reasonable grounds to believe a related foreign application exists, the examiner may requisition identification of prior art cited in that foreign application, foreign application numbers/filing dates/patent numbers, and particulars of opposition/re-examination proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide the requested information or state it is not available. Examiners should not requisition information already accessible (e.g., International Search Reports or EPO/USPTO reports available online). Requisitions for translations should be limited to cases with no viable alternative; examiners should attempt to locate an official-language version or use reliable machine translations (and state when they rely on such translations). If a translation is requisitioned, indicate which part(s) are necessary. Under PCT Article 42 some document-copy requests are restricted, but requisitions for identification of prior art or application numbers are considered compliant with Article 42. Opposition/re-examination proceedings are not considered 'connected with examination' for Article 42 purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological deposit requisitions (section 94)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may requisition amendment of the description to specify the date of deposit of biological material where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requisitions relate to inclusion in the description of the date of deposit of biological material and are covered in detail in chapter 23. Applicants must respond to such requisitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of an examiner's report — grounds and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's report may be withdrawn in exceptional circumstances where facts demonstrate a need to withdraw the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations include: report sent in error; wrong address due to CIPO error; report so uninformative it prevents applicant from recognizing defects; mailing/processing errors (missing pages, incorrect due date); report based on incorrect pages of claims/description/drawings affecting relevancy; delays greater than one month between report date and applicant's receipt where the report contains a requisition or requirement under sections 85, 85.1 or 94. Requests to withdraw must be in writing (phone requests not considered). For certain grounds a time limit applies (earlier of four months after report date and the day the applicant responds). If withdrawn, obligation to respond to requisitions is removed and the withdrawn report does not count toward the report count for continued examination; often a new report will be issued with a new response time based on the new report's date. If request concerns an allegedly improper requisition under sections 85 or 94.1, or an improperly-identified requirement under 85.1, generally the report will not be wholly withdrawn; instead the specific improperly-identified requisition or requirement may be withdrawn, removing the obligation to respond to that requisition but leaving other requisitions intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor errors in an examiner's report
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor errors (e.g., minor correctness/completeness issues, typographical errors in page/claim counts, minor incorrect citations) will not lead to withdrawal of a report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the correction is not immediately obvious, applicants are recommended to raise the issue with the examiner via applicant-initiated interview so the correction/clarification is documented in an interview record; applicants may also discuss the minor error in their response to the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional drawings (section 27(5.2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner may require further drawings if those on file do not clearly show all parts of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a request is made by notice under section 27(5.2). If a good faith reply attempting to provide the requested drawings is not received within three months of the request date, the application is deemed abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of national phase translation
rubrics_metrics.description: For PCT national phase entries, if the Commissioner or examiner has reasonable grounds to believe the submitted translation contains errors, they may issue a notice to inform the applicant of the errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections must be received prior to issuance of a notice of allowance or conditional notice of allowance, unless that allowance is later withdrawn or set aside. Failure to respond to correction requests can affect new matter analysis if subsequent amendments rely on the erroneous content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of priority documents (section 76)
rubrics_metrics.description: If consideration of a priority document in a language other than English or French is necessary, an examiner may request an English or French translation of part or all of the document; if suspected inaccurate, a certified translation may be requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both notices require a response within four months; failing to respond may be treated as withdrawal of the associated request for priority (see section 7.05 for more information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of priority documents
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications claiming priority from filings made before October 30, 2019, an examiner may require within four months either a certified copy of the priority application with a certificate indicating filing date or a digital copy to be made available in the designated digital library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the request is not met the priority request will be considered withdrawn unless the applicant requests restoration of priority and provides evidence of having submitted the request to the filing office; in that case the requested documents must be provided to the Commissioner within three months after the applicant receives the evidence from the filing office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requiring a request for continued examination (section 85.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain examiner's reports should include a statement informing the applicant of the need to request continued examination under section 85.1 of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a report fails to inform the applicant and that information should have been present, the examiner will issue a separate notice. To avoid abandonment under paragraph 132(e), the applicant must request continued examination and pay the prescribed fee no later than four months after the date of the notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews — general rules and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews may take place between examiners and the appointed patent agent, common representative, single applicant, or authorized registered foreign practitioner, subject to conditions in the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent agent is appointed, the agent must be present at interviews or have provided written permission for others to attend; registered foreign practitioners require written authorization on file. If no agent is appointed and none required, only the single applicant or common representative may have an interview (they may not authorize anyone else). All interviews with examiners will be documented in the Canadian Patent Database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-initiated interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointed patent agents (or authorized persons) may request interviews with the examiner to discuss prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments must be arranged in advance. Interviews may be requested at any stage of prosecution (unless abandoned) and are conducted by the examiner in charge. During interviews, the examiner may explain defects or clarify points but will not provide definitive verbal opinions or agree to accept amendments during the interview. For interviews with an examiner in training, a senior examiner or section head will also attend. Interviews do not replace normal prosecution; any amendments must still be filed in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner-initiated interviews and Patent Examination Interview Service
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Examination Interview Service promotes direct communication between examiners and patent agents/unrepresented inventors via phone or online platforms to advance prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are encouraged to contact agents where advancement is likely (e.g., only a few minor defects remain). The service allows discussion of identified defects, suggestions for overcoming them, and correction via voluntary amendment within a predetermined timeframe. Voluntary amendments submitted after such interviews are reviewed expeditiously; if the amendment brings the application into compliance, it may be approved for allowance. The predetermined timeframe does not affect the standing of the application; if no voluntary amendment is received, the examiner will issue a report based on the last received amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract requirements (section 55)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must contain an abstract (in English or French, same language as the application) that provides a concise summary of the disclosure in the description, claims and drawings and meets specific content and form requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 55 requires the abstract to: contain a concise summary of the disclosure and where applicable include the chemical formula that best characterizes the invention; specify the technical field; be drafted to allow clear understanding of the technical problem, the gist of the solution, and the principal use(s); be suitable as a scanning/searching tool; and be no more than 150 words. The abstract must start on a new page with a separate heading and avoid patent jargon so technicians, scientists and others can understand it. The abstract must not refer to merits or speculative applications or compare the invention with the prior art. Abstracts may contain chemical or mathematical formulae but must not contain drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference characters and identifiers in abstracts (subsection 55(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Features mentioned in the abstract and illustrated by a drawing may be followed by a reference character; in biotechnology, sequence listing identifiers (e.g., 'SEQ ID NO:1') may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference characters placed between parentheses may be used to link abstract text to drawings or sequence listings where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of abstracts and limits on their use (subsection 55(7)–(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts are examined for conformance with section 55 but cannot be taken into account for interpreting the scope of protection sought or obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abstract cannot form the basis of support for subject-matter not present or reasonably inferred from the specification and drawings as originally filed. The Commissioner may amend or replace a non-compliant abstract. Typically a non-compliant abstract is identified as a defect under subsection 86(2), but if an abstract is the only obstacle to allowance the Examiner will directly amend or replace it prior to approving the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and disclosure general requirements (subsection 27(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The description, together with the claims, form the specification; the description must provide a clear and complete disclosure so the POSITA can identify what has been invented and be enabled to practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities emphasize disclosure is the quid pro quo for patent exclusivity. The description must answer 'What is your invention?' and 'How does it work?' so that, at the expiry of the monopoly, the public (POSITA) can make the same successful use of the invention using only the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory elements of proper disclosure (subsection 27(3) specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 27(3) requires that the specification must correctly and fully describe the invention and its operation or use; set out clearly the steps of a process or method of constructing/making/using a machine/manufacture/composition in full, clear, concise and exact terms enabling the POSITA; explain the principle and best mode of a machine; and for processes explain any necessary sequence of steps to distinguish the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description must be correct (clear and accurate), free from avoidable obscurity or ambiguity, not contain erroneous or misleading statements intended to deceive, and must enable the POSITA to construct or use the invention without undue trial and experiment. Quotations from case law (e.g., Consolboard and Minerals Separation) are used to illustrate these obligations.
